summary: Describes the need for a new IANA Diameter command code for a vendor-specific application that invokes policy processing, such as policy evaluation or enforcement. It supports the PEM-1 interface in the Open Mobile Alliance's Policy Evaluation, Enforcement and Management enabler. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers sometimes need to ask, is this allowed? This paper asks for a new message type so a mobile standards group can send such questions.

questions: what diameter codes does peem use
how does policy processing work in diameter
subtitle: Diameter codes for mobile policy evaluation

tldr.problem: Mobile networks need a standardized way to ask for policy decisions about whether to allow a service. The Open Mobile Alliance's PEEM system requires this capability.
tldr.mechanism: This document requests a new Diameter command code and application identifier from IANA, establishing a vendor-specific Diameter application that carries policy requests and responses between the network elements.
tldr.outcome: The request enables mobile operators to build policy enforcement systems that use the Diameter protocol as their foundation, following established telecommunications standards.

today: RFC 5224 is an Informational RFC that registers Diameter codes used in mobile telecommunications. It has not been obsoleted, and the codes remain in active use by operators deploying PEEM policy systems.

sections.title: Why Diameter for Policy
sections.content:
The Diameter Base Protocol (RFC 3588) is a messaging system used widely in telecommunications for authorization and accounting. The Open Mobile Alliance's Policy Evaluation, Enforcement and Management (PEEM) system needed to send policy requests and responses across networks. This document describes adding a new application on top of Diameter for this purpose: the Diameter Policy Processing Application.

The application is vendor-specific, using a vendor identifier (PEN) and a new command code called PDR/PDA (Policy Data Request/Answer) to distinguish these messages from other Diameter traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a system that sends questions to ask if something is allowed. Diameter is the standard way to send those questions in telephone networks, so we just need to add the right labels to make it work.

sections.title: The PEEM Interface
sections.content:
The application implements the PEM-1 interface, which is the part of the PEEM specification that handles request and response exchanges. The PEEM system controls how policies are evaluated (whether a service is allowed) and enforced (whether the network delivers it). By standardizing the Diameter codes, the document allows different vendors to build compatible systems.

Input to policy processing is passed through a new Attribute-Value Pair (AVP), and results come back through the same AVP combined with an Experimental-Result AVP that carries status information.
sections.plainLanguage: The PEEM system has one job: answer whether something should be allowed. This paper sets up the right message codes so everyone uses the same question format.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The document registers three values with the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority: a Command Code (314 for PDR/PDA), an Application Identifier (16777243), and uses the value 1 for the Policy-Data AVP in the OMA Vendor-ID namespace. These registrations ensure that no two vendors use the same code for different purposes, preventing message confusion on the network.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA is the group that hands out unique numbers so different companies don't accidentally use the same code and break everything. This paper asks for three permanent numbers.

references.text: Calhoun, P., Loughney, J., Guttman, E., Zorn, G., and J. Arkko, "Diameter Base Protocol", RFC 3588, September 2003.
